title: Every Spiritual Blessing in Christ
summary: After a brief greeting, Paul breaks into praise of the Father, who has blessed believers in Christ: chosen before the foundation of the world, adopted, redeemed through his blood, forgiven, let in on the mystery of his plan to bring all things together in Christ, and sealed with the Holy Spirit. He then prays that his readers will know the hope of God's calling, the riches of his inheritance, and the power that raised Christ from the dead and seated him far above every authority, as head over all things for the church.
story: Ephesians opens not with a problem to solve but with praise. Paul steps back to look at the whole sweep of God's purpose, from before creation (v. 4) to the fullness of time (v. 10), and places his readers inside it. Most of them were Gentiles who had once been outsiders to Israel's promises; this chapter tells them that the blessings promised to God's people are now theirs in Christ. The first half is praise for what God has done; the second half is a prayer that they will grasp it. The chapter ends on the risen and exalted Christ, which prepares for chapter 2, where Paul shows that the same power that raised Christ has raised believers from spiritual death.
historical:
The letter is addressed to the saints in Ephesus (v. 1), though the words in Ephesus are missing from the earliest manuscripts, which has led many scholars to think the letter was meant to circulate among several churches in the Roman province of Asia (see the introduction). Paul writes as a prisoner (3:1; 4:1; 6:20), most likely in Rome in the early 60s AD if the letter is his; scholars who think it was written by a follower in Paul's name usually date it later in the first century.

Ephesus was the leading city of the province and a center of the worship of Artemis, whose great temple drew pilgrims and wealth. Acts 19 describes the city as a place where magic was widely practiced and where Paul's preaching led many to burn their books of spells. Readers from that world knew what it was to live among powers: gods, spirits, fate, and the unseen forces believed to rule the stars. Paul's claim that Christ is seated far above all rule and authority, power and dominion (v. 21) would have spoken directly to them.
cultural:
Letters in the Greek and Roman world normally opened with the sender's name, the recipients, a greeting, and often a thanksgiving or prayer. Paul follows the pattern but fills it with Christian content. Instead of the usual thanksgiving he begins with a blessing, a form familiar from Jewish prayer, which praises God for his acts: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (v. 3).

Several images come from ancient social life. Adoption (v. 5) was a legal act in Roman society by which a person gained a new father and the full rights of an heir. Redemption (v. 7) was the language of buying back a slave or captive. A seal (v. 13) was an impression in wax or clay that marked ownership, guaranteed the contents of a document, or protected goods from tampering. And the pledge (v. 14) was a commercial term for a down payment, the first installment that guaranteed the rest would follow.
literary: Verses 3 to 14 form a single long sentence in Greek, one of the longest in the New Testament, piling phrase upon phrase in praise. English translations break it up, but it is best read aloud as one sweeping act of worship. Three refrains help organize it: “to the praise of His glorious grace” (v. 6) and “to the praise of His glory” (vv. 12, 14). Many readers see a Trinitarian shape: the Father who chooses and plans (vv. 3-6), the Son in whom we have redemption (vv. 7-12), and the Spirit who seals and guarantees (vv. 13-14). The phrase in Christ, or in him, recurs throughout. Verses 15 to 23 shift to prayer, which rises in its own way to a climax on the resurrection and exaltation of Christ, drawing on Psalm 110:1 (seated at God's right hand) and Psalm 8:6 (everything put under his feet).

outline.t: Chosen and adopted by the Father
Redeemed in the Son; the plan to unite all things in Christ
Paul's prayer for wisdom and revelation
Christ raised, exalted, and made head over all for the church

doctrines.note: God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world and works out everything by the counsel of his will (vv. 4, 11). Paul presents this as cause for praise, grounding believers' confidence in God's purpose rather than their own.
The Father plans and blesses, the Son redeems, and the Spirit seals. The chapter shows the three persons at work in one salvation, a pattern later confessed as the doctrine of the Trinity.
Salvation is described in rich images: adoption, redemption, forgiveness, inheritance, and sealing. Its source is the riches of God's grace, which he lavished on us (vv. 7-8).
The church is Christ's body, the fullness of him who fills all in all (v. 23). It is not merely a gathering of individuals but the community through which Christ's rule becomes visible.

words.note: Proorizo, to predestine or decide beforehand. It appears twice here (vv. 5, 11). In both places the destiny in view is positive: adoption as God's sons and life for the praise of his glory. The word says God's purpose comes first; how that relates to human choice is debated (see the hard question).

Anakephalaioomai, to sum up or bring together under one head. In verse 10 it describes God's plan to gather all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ. The only other New Testament use (Romans 13:9) is for summing up the commandments in one. The word pictures a scattered and divided creation reunited around Christ.

Arrabon, pledge, deposit, or down payment. A business term for the first installment that guarantees full payment later. The Spirit is the pledge of our inheritance (v. 14): his presence now is a real share in the life to come and a guarantee that the rest will follow.

Epouranios, heavenly; in this letter, the heavenly realms. The Greek phrase for in the heavenly realms appears five times in Ephesians and nowhere else in the New Testament. It refers to the unseen spiritual world, where believers are already blessed (v. 3), where Christ is seated (v. 20), and where hostile powers also operate (6:12).

christ: Christ is the center of the whole chapter. Every blessing is in him; the Father chose us in him, adopted us through him, and redeemed us by his blood. God's plan for history is to bring all things together in Christ (v. 10). Paul's prayer ends with Christ raised from the dead and seated at God's right hand, far above every power and every name, not only in this age but in the one to come, with everything placed under his feet (vv. 20-22). These words draw on Psalm 110 and Psalm 8, which the New Testament reads as fulfilled in Jesus. The one who died and rose now rules over all things, and he does so for the church, which is his body.

hard.q: If God chose and predestined his people before the world began, what room is left for human choice?
hard.a:
Christians who fully accept this chapter read it in different ways. The Reformed or Calvinist tradition understands it to teach that God, out of free grace, chose particular people for salvation before creation, not because of anything foreseen in them; faith is the result of that choice, not its cause. The Arminian and Wesleyan traditions, and many others, understand God's choice as based on his foreknowledge of those who would believe, or emphasize that God chose Christ as the elect one and that people are chosen in him as they come to him by faith. A third reading, often called corporate election, notes that the pronouns are plural and argues that God chose a people, the church in Christ, rather than naming individuals.

All of these views agree on what the chapter says plainly: salvation begins with God's gracious initiative, it is centered in Christ, and it is meant to produce holiness and praise rather than pride or fear. Paul writes the passage as worship, not as a puzzle to be solved. How divine choice and human responsibility fit together is a second-order question on which faithful believers disagree.

questions: Paul begins by praising God for what he has already given. How might starting there change the way you pray?
Which of the images in verses 3 to 14 (chosen, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, sealed) means the most to you, and why?
Paul prays that the eyes of your heart may be enlightened. What do you most need to see more clearly about God's calling, inheritance, or power?
